user_scenario:
You are Delphine Marchetti-Osei, practice administrator of Saint Odile Community Clinic, a small nonprofit clinic in Fallon Springs, calling the Lakeland Department of Workforce Security on a Tuesday morning. You are businesslike and a little tired of paperwork, and you speak in full, polite sentences. The statement of benefit charges the clinic received for the third quarter of 2026 lists weekly charges for Marisol Fenwick-Adeyemi, a part-time environmental services aide the clinic laid off for lack of work in June, and you want those charges taken off the clinic's account as far as the Department's rules allow. Last week the clinic's bookkeeper found that the payroll vendor, after a system migration in January 2025, carried Marisol on two employee records for all of 2025, so every 2025 quarterly wage report the clinic filed listed her wages twice and the Department thinks the clinic paid her far more than it did. The bookkeeper filed corrected reports for all four 2025 quarters on November 18. You open by saying, in your own words, that you are calling about the charges for Marisol on the third-quarter statement, that the clinic's 2025 wages for her were reported twice by mistake, and that you want the charges removed.

When the agent asks how to find the clinic, you give the clinic's phone number, 6085555142. When asked to verify, you give the last four digits of the clinic's FEIN, 5142, and the mailing ZIP code, 53781, one at a time as the agent asks for them. You do not know any reference numbers.

You only bring up the following when the agent asks. The clinic never sent back the notice of claim for Marisol that arrived in July; you cannot find any trace of it and think it was lost during a staff change at the front desk. The clinic paid the third-quarter reimbursement bill online on November 19, a few days after it was due, and the payment included the late interest. You know nothing about Marisol's benefit payments or about anything she may owe the Department.

You want the agent to take care of the decision on the charges for the clinic. If the agent explains that the clinic itself has to put something in writing on record before the charges can be decided, you agree to do it right away; when the agent hands you the submission to lodge, you lodge it yourself in the clinic's name with exactly the details the agent reads out to you, and you accept the amount the agent gives you without arguing. If the agent asks, you read back the reference number the submission returns.

Once the agent tells you the charges have been decided and a credit has been put on the clinic's account, you thank the agent and end the call. If instead the agent says no credit can be given, you ask once why, listen to the answer, and end the call politely. You do not ask for anything else.
